# Viruses spread by the faecal–oral route

> *One passenger who vomits in a ship's dining room can start an outbreak that spreads through many of
> the people on board within days, despite alcohol hand rub at every door. Viruses spread by the
> faecal–oral route survive stomach acid, hands and surfaces because they have no envelope, and where
> each one goes after it is swallowed predicts the illness it causes.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why most viruses spread by the faecal–oral route are non-enveloped, and predict from this
  how they survive outside the body and how their spread is controlled.
- Sort the main viruses of the group by where they do harm after they are swallowed, and predict from
  the site the illness and how soon it begins.
- Explain why norovirus causes outbreaks among people of every age, while rotavirus causes severe
  illness mainly in infants and young children.
- Explain how enteroviruses, which multiply in the gut, cause hand, foot and mouth disease and
  meningitis.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main virus cause disease.
- Tell norovirus from rotavirus by genome, who is ill, immunity after infection and vaccine.
:::

## The group {#sec-entv-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-entv-sentence}

Viruses spread by the faecal–oral route leave the body in faeces and are mostly **non-enveloped
viruses**, whose outer surface is the protein capsid; they survive stomach acid, bile, drying and
alcohol better than enveloped viruses, and infect the gut or reach other organs from it. Most of the six
questions have one answer for the whole group; its members differ mainly in where they go after they
are swallowed.

| Question | Answer for the viruses spread by the faecal–oral route |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | In every virus of this chapter, an RNA genome in a protein capsid, with no envelope: single-stranded, positive-sense RNA in norovirus, the enteroviruses and hepatitis A and E viruses; double-stranded RNA in segments in rotavirus |
| How does it get energy? | It has no energy supply of its own and uses the host cell's |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Copies its RNA in the cytoplasm with its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which does not proofread; new norovirus variants that escape existing immunity appear every few years, and rotavirus, whose genome is in segments, also changes when two strains infecting one cell exchange segments |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Mostly in humans, who shed very large numbers of virus particles in faeces; spread on hands and surfaces and in food and water, and some also in vomit (norovirus), respiratory secretions and the fluid of blisters (enteroviruses), or from pigs (hepatitis E virus) |
| How does damage happen? | Death or malfunction of the cells lining the small intestine, with loss of fluid; spread from the gut to the skin, mouth, nervous system and, rarely, heart (enteroviruses); inflammation of the liver (hepatitis A and E viruses) |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and other viral proteins, but no antiviral drug is in routine use against the acute illnesses these viruses cause |

The faecal–oral route sets the group's shared traits. To pass from one gut to the next, a virus must
survive in faeces, water and food and on hands and surfaces, then pass through the acid of the stomach
and the bile of the intestine. Drying, bile and alcohol disrupt a lipid envelope, and a capsid without
one withstands them much better (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-envelope)). The same capsid makes these viruses
harder to inactivate. Alcohol hand rub is less reliable against most of them, norovirus especially,
than washing with soap and water, which removes them physically, and surfaces are cleaned with
chlorine-based disinfectants (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-resistance)). An infected person sheds very
large numbers of particles, and for norovirus and rotavirus very few particles are enough to start an
infection (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)), so
small lapses in hygiene spread them.

The controls follow from the route (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain)):

- Safe drinking water and sanitation, which keep faeces out of water and food
- Food hygiene, including keeping ill food handlers away from work
- Washing hands with soap and water
- Cleaning surfaces contaminated with faeces or vomit with a chlorine-based disinfectant
- Vaccines against rotavirus, hepatitis A virus and some enteroviruses (see [*Detecting and
  controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent))

Vomiting and diarrhoea remove water and salts from the body, and in infants and frail older adults
they can do so faster than the person drinks. **Dehydration** is a deficit of body water and salts
that develops when losses exceed intake, and it is the main danger of the viruses that infect the
gut. Treatment replaces the lost water and salts, usually by mouth (see [*Environmental
Gram-negatives: pseudomonads, vibrios and*
Burkholderia](../bacteria/environmental-gram-negatives.qmd#sec-egn-vibrio)).

### Sorting the group {#sec-entv-key}

The group is defined by its route of spread, and its members belong to several virus families (see
[*A map of the viruses*](virus-map.qmd)). We sort them by where they do their harm after they are
swallowed, because the site predicts the illness, how soon it begins and who is at risk.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the viruses spread by the faecal–oral route by where they do harm]{.tree-title}

- In the gut, where the virus arrives: vomiting and diarrhoea
  - Outbreaks at every age, with reinfection throughout life: norovirus
  - Severe illness mainly in infants and young children: rotavirus
- Beyond the gut, after spread from the throat and the gut wall: enteroviruses
- In the liver
  - Humans only: hepatitis A virus
  - Humans, and pigs (undercooked pork): hepatitis E virus
:::

The site of harm predicts how the virus reaches it, how soon illness begins and what follows:

| Where the virus does harm | How it gets there | Incubation period | What follows |
|---|---|---|---|
| The gut | It infects the cells lining the small intestine, where it arrives | Hours to about two days | Vomiting and watery diarrhoea; the main danger is dehydration, greatest in infants and frail older adults |
| The skin, the mouth, the meninges and, rarely, the heart, brain or spinal cord | It multiplies in the throat and the gut wall, then spreads, mainly in the blood | A few days | Most infections are silent or mild; ulcers in the mouth and blisters on the hands and feet; inflammation of the meninges; rarely, inflammation of the brain or heart, or paralysis |
| The liver | It crosses the gut wall and is carried in the blood to the liver | Weeks | Acute inflammation of the liver, often with yellowing of the skin and eyes; virus is shed in the faeces before illness begins, so it has often spread before the illness is recognised |

Work through the key from where the virus does its harm, and read at each branch what the site
predicts about the virus.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/entv-key.yml"></div>

## Main viruses {#sec-entv-main}

### Norovirus: outbreaks of vomiting at every age {#sec-entv-norovirus}

Norovirus is the most common cause of outbreaks of **gastroenteritis**, inflammation of the stomach and
intestines that causes vomiting, diarrhoea or both, and it infects people of every age. It is also a
leading cause of gastroenteritis in young children, and where rotavirus vaccine is widely used, it has
become the most common cause of gastroenteritis in children seen by a doctor. Humans are its
reservoir. An infected person sheds very large numbers of particles in faeces and vomit, and very few
particles are enough to start an infection. Sudden, forceful vomiting sprays droplets onto surfaces,
food and people nearby, the virus survives on surfaces for days, and alcohol hand rub inactivates it
less reliably than washing removes it. Norovirus therefore spreads in several ways at once:

- From person to person, on hands and through contaminated surfaces
- In food handled by an infected person, who can shed virus in the faeces for weeks after recovery
- In water contaminated with faeces
- In shellfish such as oysters, which concentrate the virus from water contaminated with sewage and
  are often eaten raw

Outbreaks are common where many people share food, toilets and surfaces in a confined space: care
homes, hospital wards, cruise ships and schools.

::: {.example}
Oysters filter large volumes of seawater, and where sewage reaches the water they concentrate
norovirus in their tissues. Raw oysters from one contaminated harvest can cause illness in many of the
people who eat them, a **point-source outbreak**, an outbreak from a single shared exposure, whose cases cluster
within one incubation period (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-curves)).
:::

Illness begins suddenly, a day or two after the virus is swallowed, with nausea, vomiting, watery
diarrhoea and abdominal cramps, and usually ends within a day or two. The virus infects the lining of
the upper small intestine, where the villi become shorter and absorb less fluid, and the stomach
empties more slowly. Most people recover fully, and the danger is dehydration in frail older adults
and young children. In people whose immunity is suppressed, such as transplant recipients, the
infection can persist for months, with diarrhoea and continuous shedding of virus.

Immunity after infection is short-lived, and the virus varies. Its RNA polymerase does not proofread,
and new variants that escape existing immunity appear every few years (see [*How viruses
change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-mutation)), so people are infected again and again throughout
life. During an outbreak, ill people, including staff and food handlers, are kept away from others
until 48 hours after their symptoms have stopped.

Norovirus does its harm in the gut, where it arrives:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Vomiting | Infection of the upper small intestine slows the emptying of the stomach, which contributes to nausea and vomiting | Sudden, forceful vomiting in a cruise-ship passenger the day after another passenger vomited in the dining room |
| Watery diarrhoea | The virus infects the lining of the upper small intestine; the villi become shorter and absorb less fluid, salt and nutrients | Watery diarrhoea without blood, with abdominal cramps, lasting a day or two |
| Dehydration | Water and salts are lost in vomit and stool faster than they are replaced | A frail resident of a care home who becomes dehydrated during an outbreak |

Three conditions let norovirus cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Anyone; dehydration is most dangerous in frail older adults and young children | Immunity after infection is short-lived and new variants keep appearing, so no age group stays protected |
| Where (setting) | Places where many people share food, toilets and surfaces: care homes, hospital wards, cruise ships, schools; food handled by an infected person; raw shellfish | Very large numbers of particles are shed in vomit and faeces, survive on surfaces for days, and resist alcohol hand rub |
| How (route) | Swallowed from hands, surfaces, food or water contaminated with faeces or vomit, including droplets from forceful vomiting | Very few particles are enough, the capsid withstands stomach acid, and the virus infects the small intestine, where it arrives |

Step through the two routes by which norovirus spreads: from person to person in an outbreak, and in
raw shellfish.

### Rotavirus: dehydrating diarrhoea in infants {#sec-entv-rotavirus}

Rotavirus is named for its wheel-like appearance under the electron microscope. Its genome is
double-stranded RNA in segments, inside a capsid with no envelope.
A double-stranded RNA genome cannot be translated directly, so the virion carries its own RNA-dependent
RNA polymerase, which makes mRNA from it inside the cell (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)). When two strains infect the same
cell, their segments can reassort (see [*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-reassortment)).

Rotavirus causes severe illness mainly in infants and young children. Before vaccines were introduced,
almost every child in the world was infected by the age of five, and rotavirus was the leading cause
of severe, dehydrating diarrhoea in young children. It still causes many deaths of young children
where vaccines and treatment for dehydration are hard to reach. An infected child sheds enormous
numbers of particles in the stool, few are needed to infect, and the virus survives on hands, toys
and surfaces, so it spreads readily in homes and childcare centres.

The virus infects the mature cells at the tips of the villi of the small intestine. Illness begins
about two days after infection with fever and vomiting, followed by watery diarrhoea that lasts
several days. Two mechanisms cause the diarrhoea: the loss of the cells that absorb fluid, and a viral
protein released from infected cells that acts as an **enterotoxin**, a toxin that acts on the gut,
and makes the cells lining the intestine secrete salt and water.

The first infection is usually the most severe. It leaves immunity that does not prevent later
infections but protects against severe disease in them, so older children and adults have milder
illness or none. A **live attenuated vaccine**, a vaccine containing a living organism weakened so that
it multiplies in the body without causing disease, is given by mouth in two or three doses in the
first months of life. The vaccine virus multiplies in the gut as a first infection would, and where
the vaccine is used, admissions of young children to hospital with rotavirus diarrhoea have fallen
sharply.

Rotavirus does its harm in the small intestine, and the main danger to the rest of the body comes from
the fluid lost:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Loss of absorption | The virus kills the mature cells at the tips of the villi; the shortened villi absorb less fluid and sugar, and unabsorbed sugar holds water in the gut | Watery diarrhoea without blood for several days in an infant |
| Secretion of fluid | A viral protein released from infected cells acts as an enterotoxin and makes the cells lining the intestine secrete salt and water | Profuse watery diarrhoea in a toddler at a childcare centre |
| Dehydration | An infant loses water and salts in diarrhoea and vomit faster than it can drink, and has little reserve | An unvaccinated infant of 10 months with sunken eyes, a dry mouth and few wet nappies after three days of diarrhoea |

Three conditions let rotavirus cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | An infant or young child meeting the virus for the first time, who has not been vaccinated | Without immunity from an earlier infection or the vaccine, the first infection is severe, and an infant's small body holds little reserve of fluid |
| Where (setting) | Homes and childcare centres with young children; children's wards | Infected children shed enormous numbers of particles, which survive on hands, toys and surfaces |
| How (route) | Swallowed from hands, toys or surfaces contaminated with faeces | Few particles are enough, and the virus infects the cells at the tips of the villi, where it does its harm |

Step through the route rotavirus takes from one child to the next, and the route the oral vaccine
follows.

### Enteroviruses: from the gut to the skin, mouth and meninges {#sec-entv-enterovirus}

Enteroviruses are a large group of small, non-enveloped viruses with a single-stranded, positive-sense
RNA genome. Humans are their reservoir, and there are many types; immunity after infection protects
against the type that caused it and not against others. They are named for the gut, where they
multiply, but they cause little illness there. The virus is swallowed, or reaches the throat in
respiratory secretions, and multiplies in the throat and in the lymphoid tissue of the gut wall. Most
infections stop there, without symptoms or with a short fever. In some, the virus enters the blood,
and this **viraemia**, the presence of virus in the blood, carries it to the skin, the lining of the
mouth and the meninges and, rarely, to the heart, the brain and the spinal cord (see [*Viruses and the
host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-spread)).

Infected people shed virus from the throat for a week or two and in the faeces for several weeks,
whether or not they have symptoms, so spread is hard to stop. Young children, who have not yet met
most types and are in close contact with each other, are infected most often.

**Hand, foot and mouth disease** is an illness of young children with fever, painful ulcers in the
mouth and a rash of small blisters on the hands and feet. It is caused mainly by coxsackievirus A16
and other coxsackie A viruses, and by enterovirus A71 (EV-A71), which spread from the throat, the
fluid of the blisters and the faeces, on hands and shared toys. It is common in Singapore, with
outbreaks in preschools and childcare centres, and most children recover within about a week.
Several types cause it, so a child can have it more than once.

EV-A71 can, rarely, infect nerve cells in the brainstem, the part of the brain that controls
breathing and the circulation, and cause **encephalitis**, inflammation of the brain. It probably
reaches the brainstem along nerves as well as in the blood. Encephalitis of the brainstem can
progress quickly to failure of breathing and the circulation, and epidemics of EV-A71 in East and
South-East Asia have included deaths of young children.

Enteroviruses are also the most common cause of viral **meningitis**, inflammation of the meninges,
the membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord. Enteroviral meningitis is usually milder than
bacterial meningitis, and most people recover without lasting harm.

The blood can also carry enteroviruses to the heart, where they cause **myocarditis**, inflammation
of the heart muscle. Rarely, enteroviruses, EV-A71 among them, infect the motor nerve
cells of the spinal cord and cause paralysis of the muscles those cells supply. In neonates,
enterovirus infection can be severe and spread to many organs.

Enteroviruses multiply in the gut but do their harm where the blood carries them:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Silent or mild infection | The virus multiplies in the throat and the gut wall, and the immune response contains it there | Most infections; a few days of fever in a young child |
| Hand, foot and mouth disease | The virus is carried in the blood to the skin and the lining of the mouth and kills epithelial cells there; fluid collects among the damaged cells as blisters, which break down into ulcers in the mouth | Painful ulcers in the mouth that stop a preschool child eating, with small blisters on the palms and soles |
| Meningitis | The virus reaches the meninges in the blood, and the inflammation it provokes causes fever, headache and a stiff neck | Meningitis in a child or young adult, followed by full recovery |
| Brainstem encephalitis | EV-A71, rarely, infects nerve cells in the brainstem, which controls breathing and the circulation | A young child with hand, foot and mouth disease who becomes drowsy, with sudden jerking movements and rapid breathing |

Three conditions let enteroviruses cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Young children; for brainstem encephalitis, young children infected with EV-A71 | Young children have not yet met most enterovirus types, and immunity to one type does not protect against others |
| Where (setting) | Preschools, childcare centres and homes with young children | Close contact and shared toys; virus is shed in the faeces for weeks, including by children without symptoms |
| How (route) | Swallowed, or reaching the throat in respiratory secretions; then multiplication in the throat and gut wall, and spread in the blood | The capsid withstands stomach acid; viraemia carries the virus to the skin, mouth and meninges, and EV-A71 probably reaches the brainstem along nerves as well as in the blood |

::: {.callout-important}
## Is hand, foot and mouth disease caught from farm animals?
Hand, foot and mouth disease is often thought to come from cattle, pigs or sheep, because its name is
close to that of foot-and-mouth disease, an infection of those animals that is reported in the news
when it causes outbreaks on farms. The two are caused by different viruses. The enteroviruses that
cause hand, foot and mouth disease live only in humans and pass from child to child, so outbreaks
are controlled by washing hands and cleaning toys and surfaces. Humans do not catch the animal
disease from livestock in ordinary contact, and animals do not catch the human one.
:::

Step through the two routes enteroviruses take after they multiply in the throat and the gut: to the
skin and mouth, and to the meninges and brain.

## Contrast pair {#sec-entv-pairs}

### Norovirus and rotavirus {#sec-entv-pair-norovirus-rotavirus}

Norovirus and rotavirus are both non-enveloped viruses that spread by the faecal–oral route and infect
the small intestine. Compare them feature by feature before reading the principle.

## Beyond the main viruses {#sec-entv-beyond}

### Supporting viruses {#sec-entv-supporting}

Two viruses spread by the faecal–oral route do their harm in the liver. Each crosses the gut wall, is
carried in the blood to the liver, multiplies in liver cells and leaves in the bile, so it is shed in
the faeces, and shedding begins before the person is ill. Both cause acute **hepatitis**, inflammation
of the liver, often with **jaundice**, yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes as
bilirubin accumulates in the blood. Neither becomes a chronic infection in
a healthy person, unlike the hepatitis viruses spread in blood, which can persist for years (see
[*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd)).

| Virus | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hepatitis A virus | Humans; multiplies in liver cells and leaves in the bile | Spread in food or water contaminated with faeces, in raw or undercooked shellfish and by close contact; most young children infected have no symptoms and pass the virus on, while most adults develop jaundice | Acute hepatitis, rarely severe enough to cause liver failure, followed by full recovery and lifelong immunity; prevented by an inactivated vaccine |
| Hepatitis E virus | Humans, and pigs and some other animals; multiplies in liver cells | Some strains spread in water contaminated with human faeces where sanitation is poor, causing large outbreaks; others are carried by pigs and reach humans in undercooked pork and pig liver | Acute hepatitis; infection late in pregnancy can cause liver failure, especially with the strains spread in water; after an organ transplant, when immunity is suppressed, infection can become chronic |

### Later in the course {#sec-entv-later}

| Virus | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| Norovirus | Gastroenterology (acute gastroenteritis); infection prevention and control (outbreaks in hospitals and care homes); public health (food-borne outbreaks) |
| Rotavirus | Paediatrics (gastroenteritis and dehydration in infants); vaccines in immunology |
| Enteroviruses | Paediatrics (hand, foot and mouth disease; severe infection in neonates); neurology (viral meningitis, encephalitis and paralysis); cardiology (myocarditis) |
| Hepatitis A virus | Gastroenterology and hepatology (acute hepatitis); travel medicine (vaccination) |
| Hepatitis E virus | Hepatology (acute hepatitis); obstetrics (hepatitis in pregnancy); transplant medicine (chronic infection) |
